t: A spade leans against the throne, its blade still bright. The Barrow-King stands between you and it.
The mud here has been heaped up and patted down, and the reeds will not grow on it. Something is buried under there.
Marta's bed. Her money box sleeps under that pillow; she would not thank you for lying on it.
Marta's bed. Her money box sleeps under that pillow; she would not thank you for lying on it.
The blanket is rough but warm. How long do you sleep?
You wake with a start. The hearth has burned down to embers and the window is black.
Outside, something heavy crashes against the fence. A laugh, low and ugly, and a second voice hushing it. Then the crunch of splintering wood.
Outside, something heavy crashes against the fence. A laugh, low and ugly, and a second voice hushing it. Then the crunch of splintering wood.
Someone is in the yard. Your pitchfork leans against the wall outside, by the door.
Someone is in the yard. Your pitchfork leans against the wall outside, by the door.
We have done our business, you and I. Forget my face.
I have nothing more for you. Walk on.
Travelling light? Wise. The roads have ears.
The old man has read it, then. Paper can still burn. People too. Good day.
A sensible soul.
Then may Dunhollow bury you with it.
I carry nothing for anyone. Thirty-five.
You carry a letter sealed with a B. My master would pay handsomely to have it back, unread by village elders. Thirty-five copper. More than those farmers will ever give you.
Huh. There are still some of you left. For the road. And watch the man in grey.
Smart. Tell the old man we were too many.
An elf, running Hamond's errands? The Baron would pay good silver for ears like yours. Lucky for you I don't work for him on Sundays.
Hamond's errand-runner. Before you swing that thing: my people were colliers in these woods until the Baron burned us out. Now we rob for him, because he pays and nobody else does.
So. You can bleed for an old man's village. Or you can walk away twenty-five copper richer. Or, if you have a heart in there, let us leave this valley tonight and never come back.
They squirm and nip all the way. Marta will know what to do.
Where Old Greymaw fell, you hear a thin whimper. Under the roots of a fallen pine: three wolf pups, eyes barely open, pressed against each other.

They are too small to survive alone. And far too small to be dangerous. For now.
You let me warm his supper for weeks. Go away. …No. Stay a moment. Then go away.
You tell her. The city was a lie. Edric is in the churchyard. He has been all along.
Then I'll go to them. Today.
The Well Sisters? My mother used to go. I thought it had died out with her. Washday. I'll go on washday.
Good. Then I can stop watching that road.
The goblins on Collier's Trail. Are they still out there?
Of course he did. Stubborn fool. Two of them and a handcart.
Quick. Good. Thank you for not letting me imagine the rest.
The goblins. On the trail. Are they…?
And the ones who did it?
Goblins. He always said they never come out by day. Are they still there? On the trail?
I knew it. He always said he'd sell the charcoal there. I'll wait.
Ada sees the knife in your hand before you say a word. Two letters are carved into the handle: and .
Ada sees the knife in your hand before you say a word. Two letters are carved into the handle: and .
No. Don't say it yet. Let me look at you first.
You found him. Didn't you. Where is he?
Any news?
He took the handcart south from the crossroads, down Collier's Trail to the charcoal pits. Hobb the carter saw him turn onto it. Eight days ago now.
Thank you. Whatever it is, I would rather know. Folk say goblins have been seen on that trail. Be careful.
My husband Edric took our handcart to the charcoal pits eight days ago, to buy charcoal for the winter. He hasn't come back.
Hobb the carter saw him at the crossroads, turning south onto Collier's Trail. That's the last anyone saw of him. You're armed. Would you look for him? Please.
I KNEW it. I'll write one about you next!
Terrible… but memorable? I can work with memorable.
A patron of silence! That's a first.
An ELF! A real elf! You people invented music, didn't you? Then you must judge my new song! Ahem.
Friend! Judge my new song! Ahem.
Ohhh the goat, the goat, the goat went up the hill / and then the goat, the goat, the goat stood very still…
Bitten twice? He likes you, then. Here, bread and a coin for your trouble.
Buy him? BUY Barnabas?
She thinks.
…Deal. He's yours. You'll regret it.
You hand him straight to Marta, who is delighted.
…He does, doesn't he.
Barnabas! Get down off my roof, you wretch! Look at him, eating my thatch!
Elf, are you? Good. You lot are supposed to be good with animals.
That's Barnabas. Third time this week. He'll eat the whole roof and Hamond will blame me. Get him down, would you? Carefully, he bites.
Bless you. Bring a light. And maybe don't bring the ring, if you've got it.
Something weeps in the yard at night. At Edric's grave. I've buried folk sixty years and never heard the dead complain.
The elder says it's owls. The elder doesn't sleep next to a graveyard. Come after dark, would you? See what it wants. I'll pay what I can.
Quiet as a church, last night. Here. Ten coppers, and I'll dig your grave for free when it's time. Not soon, I hope.

Found this in the old crypt when I dug for Edric. A fen-woman's bodice, black and frayed, smelling of peat. Whoever she was, she was buried proud. Didn't feel right selling it. Feels right giving it to you.
Don't bring it back. Ever.
So you're learning from her. Hm.
Dug it out of the old ossuary, under the chapel. Bones bound to a yew pole. I've not slept right since it came in the house. Sixty coppers and it's yours, and good riddance.
Quiet week. Nobody's died, and nobody's come back. That's how I like it. Ada's man still not home? Collier's Trail's no place to be alone, these days.
Don't argue.
The ring comes off easily. It is warm from the earth. Behind you, somewhere, a spade stops scraping.
Thank you for telling me straight.
An old man leans on a spade beside a fresh mound of earth. The wooden marker reads EDRIC.

Hobb and I fetched him on a borrowed barrow, after you found him on Collier's Trail, poor lad. I buried him proper. He had a gold ring on him. I left it on. Sixty years digging, I never took a thing from the dead. My back though… my back's done. Help an old man finish the stones?
Jaws like that in an honest wood. Good riddance.
And this: watch the ground, not the beast. The ground tells you where it's going before it knows.
Old Greymaw. Twenty, and a fair price.
Heel first. Then the outside of the foot. Breathe out when you step.
Jaw traps. Iron, big enough to take a man's leg. Somebody's been setting them on the Old Elven Road for the Baron's furriers.
I found an elf in one last spring, near dead. I'd break every one of them, but the man who sets them knows me. He doesn't know you.
Old Elven Road, past the Mistmere. Green hood, a bag of chains. He'll be checking his jaws at the west edge.
Eat. You look like you need it.
The pack follows an old grey brute the others call Greymaw. Kill him and the rest scatter. Go by day.
Deer are coming back. Give it a year.
Elf. Thought I heard nothing coming.
Sit. The log doesn't bite.
You again. Good.
Mara says hello, friend. The village pays us too now. Funny how that works.
Guards! GUARDS!
This… this is the Baron's own hand. Ordering murder. I was never here.
Written, you say? To the lords? Measurements are so often wrong. Such a pity.
Sensible.
He drives in the last stake and hangs the Baron's banner from it. As he leaves, a paper slips from his satchel into the grass.
By order of Baron Bertram of Hollowmere, these boundary stones are hereby corrected. Dunhollow's common pasture now belongs to the Baron. Nothing personal. Just measurements.
Took it off his man in grey, the night we left. His orders to burn us out, in his own hand. Do something useful with it.
You let us go. So we came home instead of running. The Baron thinks we're gone. Let him think it.
Forty years I burned charcoal here. Then the Baron's men came with torches. Now… Now we burn it again. Thank you, stranger.
Behind you! The wolves first, then the trap!
The jaws bite your fingers before they give. Faelan drags his leg free and breathes for a while. Then he presses a silver leaf into your bloody hand.
Show this at the Silver Gate, north of the mere. They will know you as Faelan's friend.
Go, then. I will remember your face.
Someone did, and then they left.
A young elf lies in the reeds, one leg caught in an iron trap. The Baron's mark, a crude B, is stamped into its jaws. His face is grey with pain, but his eyes are sharp.
Kinsman? Here, among the axes? Then the stars have not forgotten me after all.
A human. Have you come to finish what the trap started, or to open it?
Walk in the light of the lanterns, kinsman. Sylvhaven is beyond the arch.
You carry Faelan's leaf. The gate is open to you, friend.
The axes are quiet. The gate remembers who quieted them. Pass.
Faelan gave this to you himself. Then the gate already knows you. Keep it close: in Sylvhaven it speaks for you.
Faelan lived. He crawled home on his hands. He will not forgive you, and he should not. But a thief who comes back is rarer than a friend. Pass, and be watched.
The Fellings are quiet, and the birds went back to the silver trees. We saw who did it. Pass.
East of the mere, men of the Baron of Hollowmere are cutting down our silver trees and floating them south to sell. Each of those trees is older than your kingdom.
Stop the axes, and the gate will know your face.
I have guarded this arch for three hundred years. What would I buy with that? A hat?
You carry the stink of the mere, and of Faelan's fear. The gate is closed to you.
We found one of ours in the reeds, too late. The wolves had him. Were you there? The mist says you were.
The gate stays shut.
No one of the short-lived has passed this arch in sixty years. Tell me why you should be the first.
Four thousand and twelve, four thousand and thirteen… leaves. I count them every spring. You made me lose my place. Back to one, then.
The healers say I will dance by midsummer. Badly. I always danced badly.
The Baron of Hollowmere sells our silver trees to shipwrights in the south. His axes are in the Fellings, east of the mere, and every day there are fewer songs in the wood.
We do not shed blood lightly. You have walked among the humans, and learned to. Stop the axes.
We do not shed blood lightly. Your kind does it every day, and sometimes well. Stop the axes.
Your pack is full. Make room, and come back.
It was made before your grandfather's grandfather was born. Wear it well.
You paid them to go. They will come back when the coin is spent, and bring their brothers. Still, today the trees stand. Take this, for today.
Choose a gift of Sylvhaven.
We heard the fighting from here. Blood in the Fellings. It will grow flowers, in time.
You drove them off with their own master's crimes. You have learned the humans' ways well.
You drove them off with their own master's crimes. That is a very human kind of wisdom.
You sent them to the colliers, to cut only dead wood. Clever. Even the old trees approve.
Then an envoy will walk with the next moon. If your village is kind, we will remember it for a thousand years. If it is not… we will remember that too.
Wise, and sad. Keep our secret, then. We will keep yours.

Sixty years ago we stopped walking your roads. Your people burned a witch in Hollowmere, and we understood. If we come back, some will call us monsters. Some will call us gold. Tell me, which will Dunhollow do?
Aerwen, who keeps the lanterns of Sylvhaven. We are the last of the elves west of the mountains. The rest sailed, or sleep, or forgot us.
Your village and mine were friends once. The shrine in the mere remembers, even if nobody else does.
By the fourth verse he is taking notes. By the ninth he is weeping.
Who wrote this? Pip? PIP? I must commission him. Take this to him.
He gives you twelve copper, which you do not give to Pip.
In… pies.
Mostly? Then some of you are not. I will write a poem about the ones who are not.
One of us, who grew up among the humans! You must tell me everything. Is it true that they put cheese on bread? On purpose? And sing songs about animals?
A human! A real one! Tell me, is it true that your people put cheese on bread? On purpose? And sing songs about animals?
An old elf sits alone by the dead pool. The pavilions are black. The lanterns are glass and ash.
They came in the night, with torches and the Baron's banner. They knew the paths. Someone showed them the paths.
I felt it. The pool was bright for a moment, as bright as the evening she first came here, soaked to the knees, looking for her goat.
Thank you. I think I will go and sit with her awhile. Take my cloak; she always said it suited humans better.
The moonbloom is not in your pack, and it is not in the ground. It is in a market somewhere.
You have lived among the humans too long. You needed the coin more than the dead do.
Humans. You always need the coin more than the dead do.
The graveyard of Dunhollow, north of the well. Her name was Maren. Please.
Then lay this where she sleeps. If she sleeps.
I know, I knew when I said it. It helps to hear it said by one of you.
I had a friend in your village once. Maren, a weaver. She laughed like the brook. She said she would come back in the spring. That was sixty springs ago.
You grew up among them. Perhaps you know how fast they count.
You short-lived people count so fast.
Our favourite guide! The Baron sends his thanks. The shipwrights send theirs. The elves, not so much.
Murder. Of his own people. In his own hand. Lads, we were never here. Leave the logs. Leave the axes if they're heavy.
Mara Blackthorn's back in the pits? And paying? Dead wood burns hotter anyway. And it doesn't sing at night. These ones sing at night.
Thirty for a day off? You're a strange one.
They leave the logs where they lie.
Elves. Real ones? With gold?
The Baron will make me a knight for this.
Silver-oak. Four gold a trunk from the shipwrights in Saltmouth. The Baron takes three, I take one, and the trees don't complain. Mostly they don't complain.
In three hundred years this will be a forest again. Come back and see it.
Dead wood only, the lad says. Grane's lads work harder than mine and complain less. Something sings in those trees at night. Nobody cuts the live ones now.
Sylvhaven sends greetings to Dunhollow. Your elder has offered us bread. And cheese. Tirnel will be unbearable.
She would have been eighty-four. I brought her the old songs. She liked the sad ones.

This lamp post is my best friend. My only friend. Don't tell the others.
He never interrupts. Not like you.
THIEF!
A man with a cabbage in each hand points past you at a skinny hooded young woman with a loaf under her coat.
That's the third loaf this week! Grab her!
Psst. The crates behind the tannery. Nobody's watching them tonight. You didn't hear it from me.
Thanks for the bread.
You… paid for it? Huh.
The guard's glove closes on her shoulder. She doesn't cry. She just looks at you, and remembers you.
I owe you one, stranger.
It's for my brother. He's little. Please don't tell the guard.
The Crown's justice has come to Hollowmere. The statue will be recast as a horse trough. Everyone agrees this is an improvement.
…and by the grace of Baron Bertram the pasture of Dunhollow shall be improved by its annexation, for the good of the sheep, who are not consulted…

The Baron's men took off their red and put on blue. Mostly the same men. Don't tell the Magistrate.
Keep walking. The Baron doesn't like crowds that aren't cheering.

I pay better than Marta. I also ask fewer questions.
Nothing to sell? Then stop blocking my light.
Pleasure. Don't read them in public.
Pages cut out of the Steward's own ledger. What the Baron paid, and to whom. A clerk owed me money. Forty copper, and you never saw me.
Pleasure doing business.
Jory's crew? They jump everybody. It's a hobby. Give me 15 copper and they'll leave you be. Or break their heads. Either way, keep it out of my shop.
The Crown's men are everywhere now. Bad for business. Good for sleep.
The Baron's taxes made thieves of half this ward. I just buy what the other half steals.
Wear it with pride. Rats can smell fear, and straw.
Tuck's the name, rats is the game. Rats in the tannery, rats in the keep, rats in the Baron's own bed! Well. One rat in the Baron's bed. The Baron.
Tam came home! The logging crew in the east just… stopped. He says a stranger ended it. Was it you? Here. It's all I have.
My Tam went to cut trees for the Baron, east of the mere. They say there was a fight. They say… he isn't coming home.
You remember the loggers in the Fellings. You don't know which one was Tam.
My boy Tam went east with the Baron's loggers. Good money, they said. If you pass the Fellings, tell him his mother wants him home.
I'll never cut another tree. They sang, you know. At night. Mother thinks I'm mad. Maybe I am.
The Steward in the Castle Ward. Orrin. He keeps the Baron's secrets in his head and the Baron's money in his boots. Go careful.
Spare a copper for a veteran of the Baron's wars? Which wars, you ask? All of them. He loses them all.
You know my cousin Pip? The one with the goat song? The family doesn't talk about the goat song.
My cousin Pip, in Dunhollow, is the talented one. Everyone says so.
The bells rang for an hour when they took the Baron. I didn't ring them. I don't know who did.
The Magistrate from the Crown sleeps in our guest room. He is a patient man. He is waiting for someone to bring him the truth.
The keep's sealed for the trial. Nobody in or out.
The Baron sees no one without the Steward's leave. Talk to Orrin.
The keep's sealed for the trial. Nobody in or out.
The Baron sees no one without the Steward's leave. Talk to Orrin.
Our loyal friend from Dunhollow! The Baron sleeps better thanks to you. Come back if you find anything else… inconvenient.
Wise. Very wise. The Baron remembers his friends.
Want? Nothing. The Baron wants what every lord wants: more. More pasture, more timber, more tolls.
Dunhollow sits on good land and pays little tax. That is a problem the Baron is solving. Slowly. Legally, where possible.
So you are the one who chased our surveyor off the boundary stones. The Baron has heard of you. He is… interested.
A traveller from the south road. From Dunhollow, by the mud. What brings you to the Baron's door?
The trial begins at the next assize. The Crown thanks you. The valley, I suspect, will thank you longer.
By morning the red banners are down.
By morning the red banners are down.
Murder of his own subjects, in his own hand, under his own seal.
His steward's letters. Bribes, threats, a list of names. The Keep's own hand.
The Keep paid trappers to snare the King's free elves. That alone is treason.
The Steward's own ledger: every copper paid to Mara's cutthroats.
Mara Blackthorn's journal. Dates, coin, and whose coin it was.
Guard! Wake the Crown's men. We go to the keep tonight.
The old king's grant. Genuine. Then the Baron's surveyors are forgers, and his new pasture is theft from the Crown's own grant. That is enough to open an inquiry. It is not enough to hang him.

Bertram does not steal land with his own hands. He pays people. Bring me paper that shows who he paid, and for what: his orders, his steward's accounts, the bandits' books. Sella the Fence in the Lowstreets sells secrets. Start there.
You had proof, and you sold it. Then find me more. A man like Bertram leaves ink everywhere.
Proof. Everyone whispers that the Baron burns villages and hires bandits. Nobody brings me paper with his mark on it.
His orders, his steward's accounts, the books of the people he paid. Bring me any of that, and I will bring the Crown.
Aldous, Magistrate of the Crown. The King sent me to see whether the Baron of Hollowmere keeps the King's peace. So far I have seen only good wine and closed doors.
Deal! Snagtooth moving house anyway. Too many wolves. Too many YOU.
Is FRONT now. Because Snagtooth SAYS.
Oi! Big-folk! This Snagtooth hole. Snagtooth rules it. You give shiny, you walk away with all your fingers. Very generous. Snagtooth famous for generous.
Master says we're making ploughshares now instead of spearheads. Ploughshares! I hope the Crown pays as well.
Sixty spearheads for the Baron this month. Master says he'll believe the money when he bites it.
Mother says a good tunic tells the town who you are before you open your mouth. Yours says… …'mud'.
The candle catches. For a moment the chapel is very quiet, and so are you.
Rest a while. The Dawn does not ask who you fought, only whether you are tired.
Well! That grey brute has kept me out of my own mint-bed all month. I never even had to ask. Here, it's all I have made up today. Come back for more; friend's price.
West end of the pond, by the old bones. Don't let it get behind you.
Careful where you step. Not you: the wolf. A grey one has taken to drinking here at the pond's edge, and it doesn't care for company. I need the water-mint that grows right where it sits.
I heard it. Good.
Here. Thistle, honey, a little of this mint. Better than what the priests sell, and I'll tell them I said so.
The wolf, love. West end of the pond.
Back for more? The mint is good this week.
Fen-fever? Poor lamb. I'd brew it today, but I can't get to my mint with that wolf at the pond.
Drive it off and I'll have a tonic ready before you're back.
Fen-fever. Gerd's boy, is it? Went chasing lights.
Warm tonic. Make him drink all of it, however he complains. No charge: the pond is mine again thanks to you.
You again. Go on through, the gate knows your face.
He does not ask for coin. He does not explain why.
Road's the Baron's. Gate's the Baron's. Onion's mine.
I walk to the Chapel of the Dawn in Hollowmere every spring. Forty years. My knees have become a prayer of their own.
An elf in white walks slowly along the old paving, singing in a language like water over stones. She nods to you without stopping.
The lanterns know you now. Walk in their light.
The lanterns along the road stay dark as you pass.
Three coppers takes you anywhere I've been. Which is anywhere you've been, funnily enough.
Hobb's cart. Three coppers, the crossroads, Dunhollow, the Hollowmere gate, or the top of the fen causeway, where Gerd's lot cleared the oak.

They'll have taken it home. Mind the big one; they say he bites.
Goblins. Came out of the Wolfwood at dusk, took a wheel off my cart and rolled it away, cackling like it was the best joke ever told. What does a goblin want with a wheel?
Find it and I'm back in business. And you'll ride with me whenever you like.

Five coppers for your trouble, and your rides are cheap from now on. One more thing. On washdays I drive four women from Dunhollow out past the Hunter's Clearing, to the Willow Pool. Old custom, older than the chapel. If you ever go that way… make some noise first. A lot of noise.
Hah! They didn't even eat it!
No wheel yet? The goblins den beyond the Wolfwood. Follow the smell of burnt everything.
Look at the reeds on the north side, where it's trampled. Whatever it was had small feet. Very small.
Tamsin, from the water:
And it stank of smoke!
You turn your back and stammer an apology. Behind you, someone snorts. Then Maud's voice, a little softer:
Lost, then. Stay like that and listen. You're not the first to come through those willows this month, and the last one wasn't polite. Something watches from the reeds on washdays. Three times now.
Brenna, sharply:
And last washday our clothes went. The whole bundle. And Lise's mother's brooch with them, the only thing she had left of her.
You look like someone who goes where others don't. You haven't come across a silver brooch lately, have you? Maybe with some greenskins? Find out who's been at our things. Please.
Four women look at each other. Then a hail of river stones, mud and one very hard pinecone comes at your head.

By the time you can see again, they are gone, and so are their clothes. Word will reach Dunhollow before you do.

An elf. They say your folk have no shame about bathing. We have plenty. Well?
Well? Either you're lost or you're a pig. Which is it?

Maud:
The pool is old, older than Dunhollow. The water takes the tiredness out of you, if the pool likes you. It likes you now. Come and rest here whenever you need it; we'll turn our backs.
The others laugh. They each press a few coppers into your hand.
Then go, and don't come back.
Goblins,
you tell them.
A whole hoard of shiny things in their warren. They must have followed the smell of your cookfire.
Tamsin saw a silver brooch on Marta's stall. Lise's mother's brooch. Go.
Nobody speaks to you. Somebody turns their back, and it isn't to spare your blushes.

Right. No. Course not. Next harvest, then.

Come on, then. Mind the third stair, it talks.
Rematch. I'll lose quick, mind. Bertha's watching.
Morning! Bed's in one piece. Mostly. I paid for the room, and your breakfast, so don't argue.
The room? The… Ha! Done. Done, before you change your mind.
Shame. Ask again when you're braver.
Different stakes? And what are you putting up?
She pinched you. That's good. She only pinches people she means to feed.
I made you this. Horseshoe nail, bent round in the hearth. It doesn't quite close. That's so it can grow.

The only one who ever kept the key. Hollowmere is a small city.

Shut the door. No, leave it. Come here.
Your loss, sweet.

Port Fearn Arianhod. The Mother House is the one with the gold over the door. The Sister at the shrine will tell you about the Daughter, if you ask nicely and don't touch the offering bowl.

Then gold will find you. Be careful what else does.

Crystal that hums near gold? If you find it, do not sleep beside it.
The Daughter of the Ferryman. When her father rows the dead across, she keeps the fares. Gold burns on the skin of those who cheat her; it always finds its way home to those who swear to her.

Pepper from the south, saffron from the east, cinnamon from a man who swore it was the bark of a tree. It isn't.

B. Bertram. Baron Bertram of Hollowmere. He has wanted the land below the old boundary stones since my father's day. So now he sends cutthroats to bleed the farms and pay his way in.

Clear them out and the village will pay you what it can.
The wood lies north of the crossroads. Take the tunnel west out of the village, then the Mill Track. Follow the arrow with the wolf's head scratched into it.
Greymaw too? Then the shepherds will sleep tonight.

South of the crossroads, where the old charcoal burners worked. Smoke rises there most nights now. A woman named Mara Blackthorn leads them, they say.
Break that camp and Bertram loses his hands in this valley. The village will pay you for it.
Work? Bandits have been bleeding the farms along the forest road. Yours too, by the look of you.
Gone? Not dead, but gone? Mercy is a strange coin. But the road is ours.
Mara Blackthorn beaten? Then the road is ours again.
I see.
Tobb says there are men at the old boundary stones, north past the graveyard. Baron's men, with stakes and a clerk.
My father said those stones were raised when the old king gave this valley to the people who farm it. If they move, our sheep have nowhere to graze, and Bertram has his pasture at last.
I have had the path past the graveyard untied for you. I cannot ask more of you. But I am asking.
North past the graveyard. Tobb will show you the path.

…to the free folk of the hollow, the land below the stones, for as long as the stones stand. For as long as the stones stand! And you kept them standing.
Then, quieter:

Collier's Trail, where Edric fell. The blackthorn by the cart. At night, or it will not come.

She turns it over in her hands, then presses a green stone into the crook and binds it with a strip of her own hem.

Tobb fills the hole himself, and mutters something that might be a prayer. On the King's Road that night, the rope stops creaking.

That is all I have. The fen has older dead than these, if you want to see what the words can do: a hag who stole my lantern, and a drowned king under the reeds. Use it kindly. Or at least on people who deserve it.
